Remember we will be selling two mini lathes at this month’s meeting. If you would like to in on the
raffle, please give $225 (cash or cheque) to our Treasurer Barry and you will receive a ticket. The winners get to take their lathes home with them. If you don’t win, see Barry again and he will return your
money. Each lathe comes with a kit including a chuck, faceplate, live center and spur center.
We will also be donating two Lathes and kits to the Tetra Society, and two lathes to the Fraser Valley
Guild.
Thanks to Bob for organizing the raffle of the wood Bob McConnel donated. Through it we raised
$200 plus dollars for the Tetra Society. Thanks to everyone who participated.
This meeting is our AGM and we are still looking for a Treasurer. We are down to the crunch now and
really need someone to step up and fill the position. It looks like we will have an election for the positions of Members At Large. Des Wilson has kindly agreed to be Secretary. Thanks Des. This is an important meeting so please plan to attend.
Don’t forget Michael Hosaluk’s demo and class march 12th and 13th. Michael is an excellent teacher
and an inspirational turner. Everyone can learn something from Michael. Hope to see you there.
Happy Turning!
Bill

Don Hoskins
1926 - 2016
It is with deep sadness that I report that Don Hoskins, a founding member of our Guild and Outstanding Contribution Award recipient passed
away peacefully last Wednesday evening six weeks short of his 90th birthday. He is survived by his wife, Daphne and four children. A memorial
will be held in March and Guild members will be notified. Our sincere
condolences go out to his family.

The Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild will hold
their Annual General Meeting on Wednesday, Feb. 24
at 7:00 at the Sapperton Pensioners Hall. All members in good standing are encouraged to attend.
Guests are welcome but may not vote. In addition to
general business there will be and election of officers
for the next year. Minutes of the 2015 AGM are presented below:
Minutes for Annual General Meeting Held at
Sapperton Hall on Wednesday February 26,
2015.
The President, Bill Fowle, called the meeting to order at
7:23pm.
50 members in good standing were in attendance for
the meeting and a quorum was declared.
Bill Fowle asked for a motion to accept the minutes of
the 2014 AGM. Gerry Vickers proposed the motion to
accept which was seconded by Bruce Campbell. A vote
was called and the motion carried.
Ken Kimberley reviewed the financial results for the
2014/15 fiscal year and presented the budget for
2015/16 (copies attached). Merv Graham proposed a
motion to adopt the financial reports which was seconded by Jim Johnson. A vote was called and the motion carried.
Old Business-
none.
New Business-
Elections of Officers.
Bill Fowle identified that the board positions of Vice
President and Treasurer were both open as well as
three Members at Large (MAL’s) and he requested
nominations from the floor for individuals to fill these
positions.
For the position of Vice President Ed Pretty nominated
Dan Breck, seconded by Claudia Hayward. No other
nominations came forward therefore Dan Breck was
acclaimed to the Vice President position.
For the position of Treasurer Ken Kimberley nominated
Barry Wilkinson, seconded by Ed Pretty. No other
nominations came forward therefore Barry Wilkinson
was acclaimed to the Treasurer position.
Four names were put forward for the three MAL positions.
John Spitters, nominated by Jim Johnson, seconded by Olaf Lepper.
Brian Lunt, nominated by Ed Pretty, seconded
by Art Liestman.
Tom Byrom, nominated by Ross Pilgrim, seconded by Merv Graham.
Phil Vetra, nominated by John Spitters and
seconded by Gerry Vickers.
A ballot was arranged with all members voting resulting in John Spitters, Brian Lunt and Tom Byrom being
elected to the three MAL positions.
The full board of directors for the Greater Vancouver
Woodturners Guild for the 2015/16 is:
President: Bill Fowle
Vice President: Dan Breck
Treasurer: Barry Wilkinson
Secretary: Bob Askew
MALs: Tom Byrom, Claudia Hayward, Olaf
Lepper, Brian Lunt, John Spitters, Des Wilson.
7. Bill Fowle asked for a motion to destroy the ballots
which was forthcoming from Allan Cusworth and seconded by Robert Carlson. A vote was called and the
motion carried.
8. Maarten Meerman proposed a motion to adjourn
which was seconded by Art Rock. The motion carried
and the meeting closed.
Minutes taken by Bob Askew, Secretary

It’s Our Turn:
The Art of the Turned Wooden Form
June 1 – June 26, 2016
At The Gallery at Queens Park in New Westminster
The GVWG will be hosting an exhibit of our members’ work for the month of June
at the Gallery at Queens Park in New Westminster. We would like to see pieces
from as many guild members as we can fit in the gallery.
To coordinate the exhibit, members are asked to send photos/details of their own
favourite works to the organizing committee by April 30, 2016 ( itsourturn@gvwg.ca ). The number of pieces accepted will depend on the number of
participants. Wall hangings and items that can be hung from the rafters are encouraged to maximize the usage of display space in this small gallery.
Volunteers will demonstrate turning techniques every Saturday and Sunday afternoon in June between 1:00 -5:00 p.m. at the Gallery in Queens Park adjacent to
Centennial Lodge. Other volunteers will be available in the gallery during the
same hours to answer questions about the works on exhibit and general questions
about the art form.
It is sure to be an exciting exhibit, showcasing work by new turners through to
seasoned professionals. There will be lots of opportunity for people to experience,
learn, and appreciate the “Art of the Turned Wooden Form”. Please plan to join us
in June for the free exhibition and demonstrations.
More details regarding participation will be circulated to guild members through
our regular bulk email system or email itsourturn@gvwg.ca

First up was a jig I used to make an East Indian traditional spice crusher. My customer gave me a 3.5”
square that was already cut the length needed but I
needed a steady rest to dampen vibrations. The problem is that the stock was square so I made this attachment that grabs the square stock on the inside and give
a smooth round surface on the outside for the steady
rest to ride. I held it timber with Cole Jaws at the headstock, attached the jib in the middle and ran up the tailstock to add more support (no point in the live center).

?We moved on to a discussion on dust collection and in
particular, separators. There are plans on the internet
for a device called a Thien or top hat Separator (see
http://www.jpthien.com/ ). It can be sized to put on a
garbage can or fibre drum (35 gal. fiber drums can be
got at Midland Liquidators for around $35.00).
You can also build a cyclonic separator which some find
more efficient and effective. See plans for this device
at: http://billpentz.com/woodworking/cyclone/
cyclone_plan.cfm
The hose that is often sold for dust collection is the 4”
ribbed plastic type. While it is nicely flexible it can
cause a lot of vacuum loss over longer runs due to the
irregular surface. Aluminum dryer vent pipe is much
smoother than the ribbed hose but, of course, not nearly as flexibleJ.
We talked about static build-up and the risk of dust
explosion. On the metal pipe it is a simple job to connect a piece of wire to the pipe leaning to any convenient ground. For the plastic pipe it is a little more work
to either spiral wrap a bare wire around the hose leading to a ground or running a bare wire down the inside
of the pipe. I am not a great fan of the inside wire option as it makes one more place where stuff can get
hung up.
Ceiling-mounted dust air filters are also a tool in the
fight against airborne dust. Do bear in mind, however,
that the dust that it filters is the same dust you are
breathing in. The best measure is to wear a good face
mask all the time. One that is worth a look is called
Dust-beb-Gone www.dustbeegone.com . Give it a look.
When talking about getting rid of your chips one person
said it can be set out for green pick-up at curbside. You
should check with the City bylaws on this – for sure
Coquitlam does not allow them in the green bin. However, try putting a “for Free” add on craigslist. Gardeners, landscapers, animal keepers, and so on are all looking for the very stuff we call “Waste”. Give it a try but
do try to keep any Walnut chips separate from the rest.
Walnut chips are really hard on horses.
Many thanks to Phil for running Tech Talk last month
while I did the FoF session. We will both be back at our

About Turing Tools
Phil asked me to talk about “turning tools” last
month. This is a huge topic so I warned everyone
that the presentation would be pretty light on details. Still, for those just getting in to turning it is
useful to have an overview of “the arsenal”.
Before we start it is important to understand that
tool makers are highly motivated to sell tools. It
helps if they are good tools but often they are not.
If a maker can convince you that the newest wing-a
-ma-jig will solve all your problems then they are
just doing a job. And remember that “cheap” tools
are good for tool makers but often not for you. So,
as the Roman carpet seller said, “Caveat emptor”
buyer beware.
Turning tools fall into one of seven categories;
scrapers, spindle roughing gouge, parting tool,
skew, spindle gouge, bowl gouge and miscellaneous. Miscellaneous is for all those tools that are
actually one of the first six but are just so weird
they deserve their own group. For example, a ring
tool is really a gouge but it is hard to see that right
off. Similarly, a chatter tool is a scraper but, again,
it hardly makes sense to talk about it like that.
Scrapers
These are the easiest turning tools to use; put it on
the tool rest, jam it into the wood and hang on.
This will remove wood after a fashion. But, the real value and elegance for scrapers is when they are
used very gently. In the hands of someone who
knows what they are doing a scraper can remove
tiny ribbons of wood leaving a beautiful surface
behind. They also come in so many different
shapes and sizes. But, if one does not meet your
need you can always grind it until it does.
One safety note here – old metal files seem like
great candidates for scrapers. But, while they are
hard they are also brittle, thus increasing the risk
of it breaking under heavy use. Better not to risk
it. Try using an old planer blade instead. The metal will hold just as good an edge but is much tougher.
Spindle Roughing Gouge
The AAW recently went on a campaign to rename
this tools from “roughing gouge” to “spindle roughing gouge” to stress the importance of it being used
only for spindle work. The reason is that the tang
on this tool is small and the cutting edge is the
largest in our tool kit. Many turners have discovered that getting a catch with a spindle roughing
gouge can result in the tang snapping and sending
the business send of the tool flying. Yet, when
sharpened and used properly this tool is very effective. In fact, I estimate that over 85% of the commercial jobs I do are with this tool.
Parting Tool
A parting tool is designed to cut a narrow, deep slot
in a project. They vary from quite wide (around
½”) to quite thin (1/16”) but they all work the same
way; anchor onto the toolrest and plunge the tool
toward the center of the wood. Wide parting tools
can also be used to roll beads while narrow ones
can also be used as shear scrapers. In general, it is
safer to plunge in a little way and then draw back
and move over a small amount and plunge again.
Doing this repeatedly will greatly reduce friction
while reducing the risk of a binding catch (very
nasty).
Bruce Campbell
Focus On Fundamentals

Page 9
GVWG
I am not a fan of diamond parting tools. On paper
they seem like a terrific idea because the widest
part of the tool does the cutting and then the tool
tapers away to eliminate friction/binding. However, this only works if the cutting edge is ground to
the peaks of the diamond on each side. Otherwise
the tool will not cut. Unfortunately, few manufactures take the time to ensure the peaks of the diamond are at the same height on each side of the
tool. This renders the tool pretty much useless. I
recommend you do not buy this kind of parting
tool.
Skew
Skew have two bevels and are sloped at an angle
from one side to the other creating a long point and
a short point. Both these points are really useful so
it is important to keep them sharp. Some people
prefer a curved edge while others prefer a straight
one. Both work well with the straight edge having
a small advantage when using the long point and
the curved one having the advantage when using
the short point.
Several makers have skews with rounded corners
or even a half round on the short point side. These
are really nice to use but if you do not have one like
that you can easily grind/sand the corners yourself.
The main thing that makes a skew easier to use is
now long the bevel edges are. Bevels length are
measured from the edge to the heel of the bevel
and are best expressed as multiples of the thickness of the skew. A bevel length of one thickness
us pretty blunt and will be easy to control. A bevel
two thickness wide will be very hard to control, especially for a beginner. I recommend a bevel
length of about one and a half thicknesses. This
give a good cut and is fairly easy to control.
Oval skews have become quite popular with the
promise that they are easier to use. They do offer a
small advantage of keeping the contact point with
the toolrest closer to the part of the edge cutting
the wood but there is a cost. Oval skews need to be
sharpened carefully to ensure the bevel meet exactly at the crown of the rounded edges. If not, the
skew may cut on one side but not the other or may
not cut at all.
Spindle Gouge
The original spindle gouge was made by taking a
thin piece of bar stock and curving it lengthwise.
They are still made today and are sold as continental spindle gouges. If you already have a round
spindle gouge you need not buy a continental and
vice versa. But if you want/need to get a large
spindle gouge (say ¾” or bigger) the continental is
the way to go. To my knowledge, only Sorby and
Ashley Iles make these.
Most other makers cut a semi-circular flute in a
piece of round bar steel to make a spindle gouge.
The depth of the flute is important. If it is at or
near the center of the bar it is a spindle gouge. If it
is much higher, say only a 1.4 of the way into the
stock it is called a detailing gouge. Detailing gouges are much stiffer when working a long way over
the toolrest.
I recommend having a 3/8” spindle gouge and perhaps a ½” one. The smaller ones are only useful in
very special cases because the vibrate so easily.
Bowl Gouge
Bowl gouges have come a long way in the last 20
year. What defines a bowl gouge is that the flute is
below the center of the bar stock it is cut from.
How the tool performs depends a lot on the shape
of the flute. In general terms flutes fall in three
categories; “V” flute, “U” flute, and elliptical flute.
The elliptical flute is a general shape that works
well in a wide range of application while the “V”
and “U” flutes work well is special circumstances.
Over the years I have migrated to the elliptical flute
(Continued on page 10)

Page 10
GVWG
for all my bowl gouges. Again, having a smaller
3/8” one and a larger ½” or 5/8” one gives you
flexibility.
Miscellaneous
As I said at the beginning, this category is a catchall for tools that do not fit easily in the first six
groups. In here I include texturing tools (chatter,
spiralling, and knurling), ring and hook tools, captured hollowing tools (specialized scrapers), thread
chasers (another specialized set of scrapers) and so
one. What is often common with these tools is that
they are often specific to just one job. I recommend you hold off buying these until you really
know you need one. I would ever try to borrow
them from a friend to try them out before committing to buying them. Otherwise you may end up
like the rest of us – with tools we rarely/never use.
Steel
There are lots of competing claims about the quality of steel today. The industry has pretty much
moved completely to HHS steel. In fact I do not
know of any maker that still makes carbon steel
turning tools. In addition, the advances make in
powder metallurgy (PM) mean that better HHS
steels can be easily sharpened to the same kind of
brilliant edge that we used to say could only be had
in carbon steel.
For more information on a comparison of tool
steels please refer to the article I wrote in the October 2008 newsletter (on our website).
Handles
Finally, handles can make a big difference in how
easy it is to turn. If you have a smaller lathe then
you should try to have shorter handles on your
tools. Also, I find finer cuts easier to make with
smaller tools. Large handles are good for absorbing shock and dampening vibration but can also
get in the way in other applications. Several makers sell their tools without handles and a number
of makers sell various handles to take accommodate different sized tools. You can also turn your
own handles (dah!) and with just a little more ingenuity you can make them adjustable. I recommend
you take the time to access your tool handles and
adjust them to fit your situation.

This is a four sided dropped wing bowl. Instead of
"cutting off the parts that don't look like a bowl," the
corners of the turning blank are left on, these corners
serve as the feet.
Safety Notes:

The steps for turning this project involve more
risk than turning a round bowl

Tools have to be razor sharp

Lathe speed is extremely fast

The 4 spinning corners hurt if fingers get in the
way! Keep your fingers behind the toolrest.
To ensure success the blank must be square with the
sides and ends sanded before the turning starts. If the
bowl blank is not square the sides and corners will not
match. (see sample).
Choose timer with solid, tight grain and avoid
spalting, knots, bark inclusions or any sign of checks.
Leave the figured woods or exotics on the shelf until
you have turned a trial piece.
Method
1 - Find the center of the block and mark it, (this will be
the top of the bowl) again getting the center mark is
crucial
2 - Drill a 5/16" hole (for woodworm screw) to a
marked depth, this will also serve as an indication
for the inside bottom of the bowl
3 - Mount the wood on the lathe (woodworm in the
chuck) at this point I bring the tail stock up to the
blank and mark a divot, then check that this mark is
dead center, if not, I trim the blank to get exact center. True up bowl blank. This will be the outside
bottom of the bowl as well as the feet
4 - Turn a tenon (sized for chuck) (mark the new center
with tail stock) this mark will be used to help center
on jamb chuck when the tenon is removed
5 - Cut out waste area between outside of bowl and to
inside of the legs, make sure very little wood is removed from the bottom corners as these will be the
footing for bowl. You need to be very careful to avoid
getting your hands in the way of the spinning corBarry Wilkinson
A Square Bowl

Page 12
GVWG
ners. They appear as ghosts and are best seen with a
dark background and overhead light, or with a back
light. I seem to get a cleaner cut when using high
speed to cut the wings (scary fast). Use the tool rest
as a steel barrier between your fingers and the spinning wood
6 - Reverse blank and mount in chuck
7 - True up and round the top corners
8 - Hollow the interior of the bowl, mark the depth of
bowl on the exterior (helpful when removing the
tenon)
9 - Block sand the top holding the paper so if a corner
catches the edge of the sandpaper it will be pulled
away from you
Jam Chuck
Mount square bowl on jam chuck and secure with
tail stock using center marking
Turn down the tenon, make sure the legs are lower
than the bottom of bowl
Finish shaping & sanding the bottom of bowl
For safety reasons, if you have never turned a square
bowl its best to keep the size of the blank 6" x 2" or
smaller, this will decrease the chance of your fingers
getting nipped by the 'ghost' corners. I got my idea
from Larry Marley, who has a 9 minute video, which
should be viewed prior to you turning a Square Bowl
View his video at: www.marleyturned.com/
